chapter_theme: Not desiring another man's wife (பிறன்மனை நயவாமை): a man who leaves his own wife for another's trades a sweet fruit for a poor one and falls; and even the learned and the yogis, once deluded by women, cannot turn the mind back.
structure_note: Two fruit images (201, 202) for the folly of leaving one's wife for another's, then a verse (203) on how even the accomplished fall to delusion.

201.reading: Young men who lust after another's guarded wife while their own wife is at home are like someone who won't eat the ripe jackfruit and toils for the fruit of the wild date.
201.nuance: The image weighs effort against reward: a large, sweet fruit already at hand against a small fruit from a thorny palm. ஆத்த, of one's own wife, is an unusual form; it is usually taken as 'married' or 'one's own'.

202.reading: Those who don't grasp the point hide away the sweet mango they tended and raised as if it were a treasure, then climb the branch of an ill-matched sour mango and fall and break their legs.
202.nuance: The sweet mango is the wife, kept locked in the house (அறையில் புதைத்து), and the sour tree another man's wife. The verse blames the man twice: for hoarding his own wife and for climbing elsewhere.

203.reading: Even the man who has grasped the meaning, those who command knowledge, and those who stand holding the flash of light in the darkness are infatuated with women who bewilder, and cannot change a mind once bewildered.
203.nuance: The three kinds of men are taken as the learned, the knowers and the yogis who see an inner light (இருள்கொண்ட மின்வெளி); that last phrase is a yogic term I can't fix. The verse speaks of women (மாதர்) in general, not only other men's wives, and its point is that attainment gives no protection.

links.note: Both argue from the wife already at home: the Naladiyar asks why a man with a loving wife looks at another's, Tirumular calls it leaving ripe jackfruit for a wild date.
Both end the adulterer with a lost leg: in the Naladiyar the leg is cut off as the king's punishment if he is caught, in Tirumular he breaks it falling from the sour mango he climbed.

203 says even the man who has grasped the meaning, those who command knowledge and those holding the light in the dark are infatuated with bewildering women (மருள்கொண்ட மாதர் மயலுறுவார்கள்). Thiruppugazh 641 describes women who bring under their bodies' power even those on the paths of chariyai, kiriyai and yoga (சரியைக்ரியை யோகத்தின் வழிவருக்கு). Both say the spiritual path itself gives no protection against this pull.

source_issues: 203: line 3 reads மருள்கொணட, a misprint for மருள்கொண்ட.
